title: How a program starts another program
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain why starting a program takes two calls instead of one, read the exit status of a child correctly, and avoid the buffering trap that makes forked programs print duplicated output.

blocks.text: Every command your shell runs, every process a web server spawns, every build step your compiler triggers goes through the same three calls. Unusually, creating a process and running a program are separate operations here — and that separation, which looks like an inconvenience, is exactly what makes shell redirection and pipes possible.
fork: one call that returns twice

fork() creates a near-copy of the calling process. Both processes then continue from the same line, with the same variables, the same open files, the same position in the code. The only thing that differs is the return value — and that is how each one knows which it is.

blocks.caption: The shape you will write for the rest of your life
lines: perror("fork");            /* out of resources — always check */
/* PARENT: fork returned the child's pid */

blocks.title: The duplicated-output trap, and why it happens
blocks.text: Output through printf sits in a buffer inside your process until it is flushed. fork() copies that buffer along with everything else — so if the parent has unflushed text and the child later calls exit(), the child flushes ITS copy and the text appears twice. Measured: a program that printed 'A ' before forking produced 'A A ' when the child called exit(), and 'A ' when it called _exit(). The fix is one line: fflush(stdout) before you fork. This is also why child processes should end with _exit() rather than exit() — _exit() skips the flushing that belongs to the parent.
exec: replace yourself with a different program

exec does not start a new process. It keeps the process — same pid, same open file descriptors — and replaces the program running inside it. Nothing after a successful exec runs, because the code that would have run no longer exists in memory.

blocks.caption: Why the two are separate: the gap belongs to you
lines: /* This gap is the whole reason fork and exec are separate calls. */
/* The child is still 'us', so we can set things up for the new program: */
int fd = open("out.txt", O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC, 0644);
dup2(fd, STDOUT_FILENO);      /* make fd 1 point at the file */
perror("execlp");            /* only reached if exec FAILED */

blocks.text: That gap is where the shell implements everything you learned in the Linux course. Redirection is a dup2 in the gap. A pipe is a pipe() before the fork and two dup2 calls in the gap. Running as another user is a setuid in the gap. One design decision — separating process creation from program loading — buys all of it.

rows: If so, with what code? (only the low 8 bits)
Was it killed by a signal?

blocks.title: An exit code is 8 bits — verified, not assumed
blocks.text: A child that calls _exit(300) reports an exit status of 44, because only the low 8 bits survive: 300 minus 256 is 44. Exit codes must therefore live in 0-255, and by convention 0 means success. This is why the shell scripts in the Linux course test for zero rather than for a specific large number.

And a status is not a number you compare directly — it is a packed value. A child killed by SIGKILL reports WIFEXITED as false, WIFSIGNALED as true and WTERMSIG as 9. Code that reads WEXITSTATUS without checking WIFEXITED first is reading a field that has no meaning in that case.

blocks.title: Run the three calls yourself
steps: Write a program with the fork/exec/wait shape above and compile it: gcc -Wall proc.c -o proc
Have the child _exit(7) and print WEXITSTATUS in the parent — confirm you get 7
Change it to _exit(300) and predict the result before running it
Have the child call pause() instead, then from another terminal: kill -9 <pid>
Print WIFEXITED, WIFSIGNALED and WTERMSIG — confirm the second and third, not the first
Add printf("A ") before the fork with no newline, have the child call exit(0), and redirect output to a file: ./proc > out.txt && cat out.txt
Now add fflush(stdout) before the fork and run it again — the duplicate disappears
Run: strace -f -e trace=clone,execve,wait4 ./proc     (-f follows the child)
blocks.expected: You should see 7, then 44, then a signal report instead of an exit code, then a duplicated 'A' that a single fflush removes. The strace at the end shows the three calls by their real names — including clone rather than fork, exactly as the syscall lesson described.

cheatsheet: fork() returns 0 in the child and the child's pid in the parent; negative means failure
exec keeps the process and replaces the program — nothing after a successful exec runs
The gap between fork and exec is where redirection, pipes and privilege changes happen
fflush(stdout) before forking, or buffered text prints twice
Children should end with _exit(), not exit() — exit() flushes the parent's buffers too
A killed child reports WIFSIGNALED and WTERMSIG instead

checkpoint.prompt: Why are creating a process and loading a program two separate calls instead of one?

choices.A: For historical reasons with no practical benefit today
choices.B: The gap between them lets the child set up redirection, pipes, and credentials before the new program starts
choices.C: exec is too slow to combine with process creation
choices.D: Because the kernel cannot allocate memory and load a file at the same time

checkpoint.explanation: Everything a shell does between typing a command and running it — redirection, pipes, dropping privileges — happens in that gap, in a process that is still under your control.

checkpoint.prompt: A child calls _exit(300). What does the parent read from WEXITSTATUS?
checkpoint.explanation: Only the low 8 bits of the exit code survive, and 300 - 256 = 44. Exit codes should stay in 0-255 for this reason.

checkpoint.prompt: A program prints 'Done' with printf, then forks, and the child calls exit(0). Output redirected to a file shows 'Done' twice. Why?

choices.B: fork copied the unflushed stdio buffer, and the child's exit() flushed its own copy

checkpoint.explanation: The buffer is ordinary process memory, so fork copies it. Flush before forking, and have children end with _exit(), which does not flush.

checkpoint.prompt: Your parent code calls WEXITSTATUS(status) without checking WIFEXITED first. When does this bite you?

choices.B: When the child was killed by a signal, where the exit-status field holds nothing meaningful
choices.C: Only if the child forks again

checkpoint.explanation: status is a packed value. Which fields are meaningful depends on how the child ended, so the WIF* predicate has to be checked before reading the matching value.
